title: Eton Mess
subtitle: crushed meringue, whipped cream, and strawberries
excerpt: Eton mess is one of the easiest and most satisfying summer desserts. Broken meringue, whipped cream, and strawberries are stirred together at the last moment. It is meant to look chaotic. That is the point.
sourceNotes: A British summer classic associated with Eton College, where it was served at the annual cricket match against Harrow.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the meringues up to 3 days ahead. Whip cream and assemble just before serving.
recipe.temperatureNote: Meringues bake at 120C for 90 minutes, then cool in the oven. The assembled dish needs no cooking.

content.text: The meringues can be bought if you prefer -- Eton mess is a forgiving dessert and the final result is good either way. But homemade meringues have a better texture: crisper on the outside, softer within. Make them a day or two ahead to save time on the day.

items.prepNote: serve with 400g strawberries, hulled and halved -- mash half and leave half whole

content.text: Heat the oven to 120C. Line a baking sheet with baking paper.
Whisk the egg whites to stiff peaks. Add the caster sugar a tablespoon at a time, whisking between each addition until the meringue is very stiff and glossy. Fold in the vinegar.
Spoon 8 to 10 rough mounds onto the lined sheet. Bake for 1 hour 30 minutes. Turn off the oven and leave inside for at least 2 hours or overnight.
Hull and halve the strawberries. Mash about half with a fork and a pinch of sugar to make a rough sauce. Leave the rest whole or halved.

Whip the cream with the vanilla to soft peaks. Break the meringues into rough chunks. Fold the cream, strawberries, and meringue pieces together loosely -- you want streaks and swirls, not a uniform mix. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Meringues are soft and chewy throughout with no crisp exterior
items.cause: Oven too hot, or not baked long enough.
items.fix: 120C is correct -- low and slow gives the right crisp shell. If your oven runs hot, try 110C.

items.cause: Assembled too far in advance, or cream was over-whipped and released water.
items.fix: Assemble at the very last moment. Whip cream to soft peaks only -- overwhipped cream weeps faster.

content.text: Eton mess is named after Eton College in Berkshire, where it was traditionally served at the Fourth of June celebrations and the cricket match against Harrow. The dessert made a virtue of broken meringue -- the mess is the point. It is a British summer institution, eaten at garden parties, on picnic rugs, and at almost every outdoor event of the season.
